items.title: Q1 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which of the following combinations best describes the typical methodology of literary research?
items.explanation: Literary research primarily relies on textual analysis, critical interpretation, and historical contextualization rather than purely empirical or quantitative methods.

items.title: Q2 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Michel Foucault
items.stem: Who said the following? "Discursive practices are not purely and simply modes of manufacture of discourse. They take shape in technical ensembles, in institutions, in behavioural schemes, in types of transmission and dissemination, in pedagogical forms that both impose and maintain them"
items.explanation: This quotation is from Michel Foucault's summary of his 1970–1971 Collège de France course, 'The Will to Knowledge' (published in Ethics: Subjectivity and Truth), where he explains how discursive practices are embedded in institutional, technical, and pedagogical structures.

items.title: Q3 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway
items.stem: Who among the following are associated with the 'Jazz Age'?
options: Scott Fitzgerald and John Dos Passos
John Dos Passos and Sherwood Anderson
items.explanation: F. Scott Fitzgerald coined and popularized the term 'Jazz Age' in works like Tales of the Jazz Age (1922) and The Great Gatsby (1925), and alongside Ernest Hemingway he is the most iconic literary figure of 1920s Roaring Twenties and Lost Generation culture.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit I: Drama · Gustav Freytag
items.stem: Which of the following is the proper explanation of the concept of "Freytag's Pyramid"?
options: Analysis of the plot of a drama
Analysis of the characters of a drama
Analysis of the theme of conflict between a woman and two men in drama
Analysis of the different types of drama
items.explanation: Introduced by German writer Gustav Freytag in Die Technik des Dramas (1863), Freytag's Pyramid is a structural model for analyzing the five-act plot of a drama: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and catastrophe/denouement.

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Arthur Symons
items.stem: Which of the following movements was Arthur Symons referring to as 'an interesting disease' and 'an over-subtilizing refinement upon refinement'?
items.explanation: In his influential 1893 Harper's New Monthly Magazine essay 'The Decadent Movement in Literature', critic Arthur Symons characterized fin-de-siècle Decadence as 'an interesting disease' marked by 'an intense self-consciousness, a restless curiosity in research, an over-subtilizing refinement upon refinement.'

items.title: Q6 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Ezra Pound
items.stem: Who made the remark: "Great literature is simply language charged with meaning to the utmost possible degree"?
items.explanation: Modernist poet and critic Ezra Pound made this famous definition in his treatise 'How to Read' (1929) and reiterated it in ABC of Reading (1934).

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Gertrude Stein, Ernest Hemingway
items.stem: Which one of the following observations of 'Lost Generation', a term coined by Gertrude Stein, is correct?
options: German Jews who survived the Second World War and went to Israel
The American expatriates in Europe after the First World War
The Irish Freedom fighters of the early Twentieth Century
items.explanation: Coined by Gertrude Stein and popularized by Ernest Hemingway as an epigraph to The Sun Also Rises (1926), the 'Lost Generation' refers to disillusioned American writers and expatriates living in Europe (especially Paris) after World War I.

items.title: Q8 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Aristotle
items.stem: Which of the following is true of Aristotle's Critical Position?
options: Writers are likely to be mere entertainers who appeal to the emotions and passions of the audience.
Texts created by poets are almost inevitably inaccurate and defective as imitations.
The best artistic texts will be both complex and unified: every part of the work will be essential to it and will be linked to every other part.
Texts should be judged on the basis of how accurately they imitate philosophical truth.
items.explanation: In his Poetics, Aristotle argues that an ideal tragic plot must possess organic unity and completeness, such that every incident is structurally necessary and removing or displacing any part would disjoin the whole.

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Plato
items.stem: What does Socrates mean when in Plato's Ion, he says "Poets are nothing but the interpreters of gods"?
options: The poets are the markers of their poems.
The poets are acutely aware of gods in composing their poems.
The poets are divinely possessed when they compose their poems.
The poets first hear what gods say then put that into words.
items.explanation: In Plato's dialogue Ion, Socrates argues that poets do not compose through rational art or mastery (techne), but rather while out of their senses and divinely possessed by the Muse in a state of poetic frenzy.

items.title: Q10 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Hellenistic / Alexandrian Greece · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Longinus
items.stem: Of the five conditions of the Sublime, according to Longinus, the most important condition is:
items.explanation: In his classical treatise On the Sublime (Peri Hypsous), Longinus identifies five sources of sublimity in literature. He states that the first and most important condition is 'a lofty cast of mind'—the innate capacity to form grand conceptions and elevated thoughts.

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following descriptions delineate Roman a Clef (Novel with key)?
options: A novel depicting the life of an artist from childhood to maturity
A novel using the altered names of the actual people of the time
A novel describing historical incidents with fictional characters
A novel giving the effect of realism by highlighting the social problems of the time
items.explanation: A roman à clef (French for 'novel with a key') is a work of fiction in which actual historical or contemporary people and events are depicted under disguised, fictionalized names (such as Thomas Love Peacock's Nightmare Abbey or Aldous Huxley's Point Counter Point).

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Fredric Jameson
items.stem: Who among the following theorists believes that the proliferation of television images is producing a cultural condition akin to 'historical amnesia'?
items.explanation: In essays such as 'Postmodernism and Consumer Society' and Postmodernism, or, The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism (1991), Marxist theorist Fredric Jameson argues that postmodern media and consumer culture suffer from 'historical amnesia'—the loss of a genuine sense of history in a perpetual present.

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Angela McRobbie
items.stem: Which cultural analyst has combined the study of different dimensions of youth culture with commentary on developments in cultural theory and politics?
items.explanation: British cultural studies scholar Angela McRobbie, associated with the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, is known for combining feminist research on youth subcultures, girls' magazines, fashion, and pop music with broader commentary on cultural theory and politics.

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Thomas Babington Macaulay, Lord William Bentinck
items.stem: Which British administrator passed a resolution for the "Promotion of European literature and Science among the natives of India"?
items.explanation: Following Thomas Babington Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (February 1835), Governor-General Lord William Bentinck passed the English Education Act / Resolution on March 7, 1835, declaring that British government funds should be devoted to the 'promotion of European literature and science among the natives of India.'

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Nissim Ezekiel
items.stem: Who among the following has written a series of poems entitled, 'Very Indian Poems in Indian English'?
items.explanation: Indian English poet Nissim Ezekiel wrote the famous satirical sequence 'Very Indian Poems in Indian English' (including 'The Patriot', 'Goodbye Party for Miss Pushpa T.S.', and 'The Professor'), gently parodying Indian English idioms and syntax.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: How many syllables are there in the word intransigently?
items.explanation: The word 'intransigently' is divided into five syllables: in-tran-si-gent-ly (/ɪnˈtræn.sɪ.dʒənt.li/).

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · Christopher Marlowe, Robert Greene, Thomas Nashe
items.stem: Which among the following group of writers is labelled as 'University Wits'?
options: Thomas Lodge, Thomas Wilson, Walter Raleigh
John Fletcher, Ben Jonson, George Peele
Thomas Kyd, Francis Beaumont, John Lyly
Christopher Marlowe, Robert Greene, Thomas Nashe
items.explanation: The 'University Wits' were late-16th-century English playwrights and pamphleteers educated at Oxford (John Lyly, Thomas Lodge, George Peele) or Cambridge (Christopher Marlowe, Robert Greene, Thomas Nashe), often grouped with Thomas Kyd.

items.title: Q18 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: How many tales and pilgrims are there in Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales?
items.explanation: Chaucer's unfinished The Canterbury Tales contains 24 tales (including the Canon's Yeoman's Tale and two tales told by Chaucer the pilgrim: 'Tale of Sir Thopas' and 'Tale of Melibee'), matching the standard UGC-NET option '23 pilgrims and 24 tales'.

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Ferdinand de Saussure
items.stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Langue is the language system, and Parole, the individual usage.
Langue is the language usage, and Parole, the individual system.
Langue is the language in abeyance, and Parole, the individual application.
Langue is the language collective, and Parole, the individual deviation.
items.explanation: In Ferdinand de Saussure's Course in General Linguistics (1916), 'langue' refers to the abstract, shared grammatical system and rules of a language held by a speech community, whereas 'parole' refers to concrete individual speech acts and usage.

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Dale Spender
items.stem: Who among the following proposed that the English language is "man made", not 'woman made'?
items.explanation: Australian feminist scholar Dale Spender advanced this argument in her landmark book Man Made Language (1980), contending that in patriarchal societies men have historically controlled language, meanings, and linguistic norms.

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: In the UNESCO definition, a 'Pamphlet' is an unbound publication that is not a periodical and contains:
options: No fewer than 5 and no more than 48 pages.
No fewer than 10 and no more than 68 pages.
No fewer than 15 and no more than 64 pages.
No fewer than 20 and no more than 80 pages.
items.explanation: According to UNESCO's 1964 Recommendation concerning the International Standardization of Statistics Relating to Book Production and Periodicals, a pamphlet is a non-periodical printed publication of at least 5 but not more than 48 pages, exclusive of the cover pages.

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · John Milton, Euripides
items.stem: From whose work did John Milton take the epigraph to his Areopagitica?
items.explanation: On the title page of Areopagitica (1644), John Milton placed an epigraph from Euripides' tragedy The Suppliants (Hiketides), along with his own verse translation celebrating free speech as the foundation of true liberty.

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas De Quincey
items.stem: Who among the following prose writers of the Romantic period authored "On Murder Considered as one of the Fine Arts"?
items.explanation: Romantic essayist Thomas De Quincey wrote the satirical dark-humour essay 'On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts', first published in Blackwood's Magazine in 1827 (followed by a second paper in 1839 and a postscript in 1854).

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Mahatma Gandhi
items.stem: Which of the following books carried the additional title Sermon on the Sea?
options: The Religion of Man by Tagore
Essay on the Gita by Aurobindo
Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule by Gandhi
items.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi's Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule (written in 1909 aboard the ship Kildonan Castle from London to South Africa) was published in an American edition in 1924 by Haridas T. Muzumdar under the title Sermon on the Sea.

items.title: Q25 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Henry Fielding, Samuel Richardson
items.stem: Which of the following work by Henry Fielding begins as a parody of Samuel Richardson's Pamela?
items.explanation: Henry Fielding's novel Joseph Andrews (1742) begins as a comic parody of Samuel Richardson's epistolary novel Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded (1740), portraying Pamela's virtuous footman brother Joseph resisting the comical seduction attempts of his employer, Lady Booby.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Richard Steele
items.stem: How often did Richard Steele's Tatler appear every week and how many issues of Tatler in total were published?
items.explanation: Founded by Richard Steele under the pseudonym Isaac Bickerstaff, Esq., the periodical The Tatler was published three times a week (on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays) from April 12, 1709 to January 2, 1711, running for a total of 271 issues.

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Charles Lamb
items.stem: In which of the following essays did Charles Lamb first use the pseudonym/persona, Elia?
items.explanation: Charles Lamb first used the pseudonym 'Elia'—borrowed from an Italian clerk named F. Augustus Elia with whom he had once worked—in his essay 'Recollections of the South-Sea House', published in The London Magazine in August 1820.

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Makepeace Thackeray
items.stem: Which one of W.M. Thackeray's novels has the following as the closing sentence? "Which of us is happy in this world? Which of us has his desire? or, having it, is satisfied"?
items.explanation: William Makepeace Thackeray's novel Vanity Fair: A Novel without a Hero (1847–1848) concludes with these famous lines: 'Ah! Vanitas Vanitatum! Which of us is happy in this world? Which of us has his desire? or, having it, is satisfied?—Come, children, let us shut up the box and the puppets, for our play is played out.'

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Kingsley Amis
items.stem: Which one of the following novels by Kingsley Amis represents its protagonist as an 'angry young man'?
items.explanation: Kingsley Amis's debut campus novel Lucky Jim (1954) features protagonist Jim Dixon, a lower-middle-class history lecturer at a provincial university whose disillusionment and rebellion against academic pretension made him an archetype of the 'Angry Young Man' movement.

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: Which one of the following has two heroes with the same name?
items.explanation: Wilkie Collins's Victorian sensation novel Armadale (1866) revolves around two main characters—often referred to as Ozias Midwinter and Allan Armadale—both of whom bear the exact same legal birth name, Allan Armadale, inherited from their fathers.

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem: Which one of the following titles of Robert Browning's works means, 'to disport in the open air, to amuse oneself at random'?
items.explanation: In the dedication to his final volume of poems, Asolando: Fancies and Facts (1889), Robert Browning explains that the title derives from asolare, an Italian verb coined by Cardinal Pietro Bembo at Asolo meaning 'to disport in the open air, amuse oneself at random.'

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: In which one of the following Middle English poems is Hector a character?
items.explanation: In Geoffrey Chaucer's Middle English courtly romance poem Troilus and Criseyde (listed here as Troilus and Cressida), set during the siege of Troy, Trojan prince Hector is Troilus's noble older brother who defends Criseyde when her father Calchas defects to the Greeks.

items.title: Q33 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following periods of English Literature is also called 'Puritan Interregnum'?
items.explanation: The Commonwealth Period (1649–1660), between the execution of King Charles I and the Restoration of King Charles II, when England was governed without a monarch under Puritan Parliamentarians and Oliver Cromwell, is also known as the Puritan Interregnum.

items.title: Q34 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Shakespeare, John Milton, Alexander Pope, Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: In which of the following works is the character 'Ariel' an exclusion?
options: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
items.explanation: Ariel appears as an airy spirit in Shakespeare's The Tempest, a rebel angel in Milton's Paradise Lost (Book VI), and Belinda's guardian sylph in Pope's The Rape of the Lock, but does not appear in S. T. Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which of the following tales in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales deals with the murder of a child by Jews?
items.explanation: In Chaucer's 'The Prioress's Tale', a young Christian schoolboy ('litel clergeon') who sings the hymn Alma Redemptoris Mater is murdered in a Jewish quarter, but miraculously continues singing after his throat is cut through the Virgin Mary's intervention.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit I: Drama · Aeschylus
items.stem: Which combination in the following constitutes the trilogy Oresteia?
options: Seven Against Thebes, Agamemnon, The Suppliants
items.explanation: Aeschylus's tragic trilogy The Oresteia (458 BCE) consists of three plays: Agamemnon, Choephoroe (The Libation Bearers), and Eumenides (The Furies).

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which of the following characters in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost over uses formal Latinate diction?
items.explanation: In Shakespeare's comedy Love's Labour's Lost, the pedantic schoolmaster Holofernes constantly parades his learning through inkhorn terms, synonymous strings, and pretentious Latinate vocabulary.

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit I: Drama · W. H. Auden, Christopher Isherwood
items.stem: Which of the following is a collaborative work of W.H. Auden and Christopher Isherwood?
items.explanation: The verse drama The Ascent of F6 (1936) was co-written by W. H. Auden and Christopher Isherwood (along with The Dog Beneath the Skin and On the Frontier). Letters from Iceland was co-written by Auden and Louis MacNeice.

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which term among the following will be applicable to a situation in which a character initiates a scheme which depends for its success on the ignorance of the person against whom it is directed?
items.explanation: In dramatic and narrative theory, an 'intrigue' is a plot device in which a character devises a secret scheme whose success depends on the ignorance or gullibility of the person against whom it is directed, as seen in Volpone or Restoration comedies.

items.title: Q40 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Ben Jonson, Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Which of the following plays by Ben Jonson ends with the performance of a puppet play in imitation of Marlowe's Hero and Leander?
items.explanation: Ben Jonson's city comedy Bartholomew Fair (1614) concludes in Act V with Lantern Leatherhead's burlesque puppet show, which vulgarizes Christopher Marlowe's poem Hero and Leander alongside the classical legend of Damon and Pythias.

items.title: Q41 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
In the following list, which two journals relate to the field of post-colonial literature?
(a) Kunapipi
(b) Interventions
(c) Daedalus
(d) Clio
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Kunapipi (founded in 1979 by Anna Rutherford) and Interventions: International Journal of Postcolonial Studies (founded in 1998 by Robert J. C. Young) are both prominent academic journals dedicated to postcolonial literature and theory, making (a) and (b) correct.

items.title: Q42 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Derrida, Paul de Man
items.stem:
Which two of the following are associated with Deconstruction?
(a) Jacques Derrida
(b) Raymond Williams
(c) Paul de Man
(d) Jonathan Dollimore
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: French philosopher Jacques Derrida (a) originated the theory of Deconstruction in works like Of Grammatology (1967), and Yale School critic Paul de Man (c) championed deconstructive rhetorical reading in America. Raymond Williams and Jonathan Dollimore are associated with Cultural Materialism.

items.title: Q43 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Which two of the following statements are applicable to feminist criticism?
(a) Recuperate the female writers ignored by the canon
(b) Fully endorse the social construction of gender
(c) Valorize the traditional canon uncritically
(d) Mostly reject the essentialising of 'male' and 'female'
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Feminist literary criticism aims to recover and re-evaluate female writers neglected by the male-dominated literary canon (a) and largely rejects biological essentialism regarding fixed 'male' and 'female' traits (d).

items.title: Q44 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Plato
items.stem:
Following Plato, which two of the following statements about 'Phantasm' and 'Semblance' are correct?
(a) 'Phantasm' is an image, while 'Semblance' is the real object.
(b) 'Phantasm' is the real object while 'Semblance' is only a resemblance.
(c) Phantasm unlike semblance has the same proportions as the object.
(d) Semblance is 'unreal' but looks 'real' as compared to phantasm.
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: In Plato's Sophist, image-making is divided into likeness-making andfantastic art. According to this distinction as framed in the question, statements (c) and (d) are paired to contrast exact proportional representation with perspective-based semblance that appears real from a viewer's angle.

items.title: Q45 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Michel Foucault
items.stem:
Which of the following describes Foucault's views on knowledge?
(a) Knowledge is not metaphysical or transcendental.
(b) Knowledge is not a matter of perspective.
(c) Knowledge is not pure or neutral but is always from a point of view.
(d) Knowledge is unconstrained by regimes of power.
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Drawing on Friedrich Nietzsche's genealogy, Michel Foucault argues that knowledge is neither metaphysical nor transcendental (a), and that it is never pure or neutral but always situated within historical power relations and specific perspectives (c).

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Pierre Bourdieu
items.stem:
Which two concepts, developed by the French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu, have become increasingly influential in cultural studies?
(a) Dissemination
(b) Gynesis
(c) Cultural Capital
(d) Habitus
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu developed the influential concepts of 'cultural capital' (c, non-financial social assets like education and taste that promote social mobility) and 'habitus' (d, ingrained habits, skills, and dispositions shaped by social class).

items.title: Q47 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Richard Hoggart, Raymond Williams, Stuart Hall
items.stem:
The key figures in the development of British cultural studies are
(a) Richard Hoggart
(b) Raymond Williams
(c) Stuart Hall
(d) Lawrence Grossberg
The most appropriate option is :
items.explanation: Richard Hoggart (founder of the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies in 1964), Raymond Williams, and Stuart Hall—(a), (b), and (c)—are the three foundational theorists of British Cultural Studies, whereas Lawrence Grossberg is an American scholar.

items.title: Q48 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Rita Kothari, Rupert Snell
items.stem:
Who are the co-editors of Chutneyfying English: The Phenomenon of Hinglish?
(a) Jamuna Kachru
(b) Rita Kothari
(c) Rupert Snell
(d) Alastair Pennycook
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Chutneyfying English: The Phenomenon of Hinglish (2011), an influential collection of essays examining the hybrid mixing of Hindi and English in Indian popular culture, media, and advertising, was co-edited by Rita Kothari (b) and Rupert Snell (c).

items.title: Q49 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · R. K. Narayan, Mulk Raj Anand
items.stem:
Which two of the following works were published after 1947?
(a) The Dark Room
(b) Mr. Sampath: A Printer of Malgudi
(c) Seven Summers
(d) The Big Heart
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: R. K. Narayan's novel Mr. Sampath: The Printer of Malgudi (b, 1949) and Mulk Raj Anand's autobiographical novel Seven Summers (c, 1951) were both published after Indian independence in 1947. By contrast, The Dark Room appeared in 1938 and The Big Heart in 1945.

items.title: Q50 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Which of the following stylistic features characterise spoken discourse?
(a) Greater use of explicit connectives
(b) Greater dependence on non-verbal connectives
(c) Greater syntactic embedding
(d) Greater use of fillers and repetitions
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Unlike formal written prose, spontaneous spoken discourse relies heavily on non-verbal cues, intonation, and gestures rather than explicit syntactic subordination (b), and frequently features conversational fillers, pauses, and repetitions (d).

items.title: Q51 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Which two aspects of cultural diffusion in the Age of Globalization need to be addressed by pedagogy of language in general and of English in particular?
(a) Unidirectionality
(b) Multidirectionality
(c) Complex and extensive
(d) Simplistic and abbreviated
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: In the era of globalization, cultural diffusion is no longer a one-way flow from Western centers to the periphery; instead, language and English pedagogy must address its multidirectionality (b) and its complex and extensive character (c).

items.title: Q52 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Which two aspects of cultural diffusion in the Age of Globalization need to be addressed by pedagogy of language in general and of English in particular?
(a) Unidirectionality
(b) Multidirectionality
(c) Complex and extensive
(d) Simplistic and abbreviated
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: In the age of globalization, cultural and linguistic flows operate across multiple global centers simultaneously. Language pedagogy therefore needs to address the multidirectionality (b) and the complex and extensive nature (c) of cultural diffusion.

items.title: Q53 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Robert Burton
items.stem:
Which two principal kinds of melancholy are proposed by Robert Burton in Volume III of Anatomy of Melancholy?
(a) 'Love'
(b) 'Religious'
(c) 'Morbid'
(d) 'Psychic'
The correct option is:
items.explanation: In the Third Partition (Volume III) of his encyclopedic work The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), Robert Burton examines two principal species of melancholy: Love Melancholy (a) and Religious Melancholy (b).

items.title: Q54 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Sara Suleri, Nayantara Sahgal, Raja Rao, Arundhati Roy
items.stem:
Which two of the following are autobiographical narratives?
(a) Kanthapura
(b) Meatless Days
(c) Prison and Chocolate Cake
(d) The God of Small Things
The correct option is :
items.explanation: Sara Suleri's Meatless Days (b, 1989) and Nayantara Sahgal's Prison and Chocolate Cake (c, 1954) are memoirs/autobiographical narratives, whereas Raja Rao's Kanthapura and Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things are novels.

items.title: Q55 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Emily Brontë
items.stem:
Which two of the following correctly describe the features of Wuthering Heights?
(a) Flash backs and time shifts
(b) Oedipal obsessions
(c) Magic and ritual
(d) Acute evocation of place
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Emily Bronte's Wuthering Heights (1847) is celebrated for its complex dual-narrator structure using flashbacks and time shifts (a) and its vivid, atmospheric evocation of place (d) contrasting the wild Yorkshire moors of Wuthering Heights with Thrushcross Grange.

items.title: Q56 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Makepeace Thackeray, Anthony Trollope, Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902), Jonathan Swift
items.stem:
Which two of the following novels belong to the Victorian Age in English Literature?
(a) Pendennis
(b) The Way of All Flesh
(c) The Battle of the Books
(d) Barchester Towers
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: William Makepeace Thackeray's Pendennis (a, 1848–1850) and Anthony Trollope's Barchester Towers (d, 1857) were both published during the Victorian era. Jonathan Swift's The Battle of the Books (1704) is Augustan, and Samuel Butler's The Way of All Flesh was published in 1903.

items.title: Q57 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Nadine Gordimer, Alan Paton, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, V. S. Naipaul
items.stem:
Which two of the following novels deal with the theme of apartheid?
(a) Purple Hibiscus
(b) July's People
(c) Cry, The Beloved Country
(d) The Mimic Men
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Nadine Gordimer's July's People (b, 1981) and Alan Paton's Cry, the Beloved Country (c, 1948) are both landmark South African novels that directly confront racial segregation and apartheid. Purple Hibiscus is set in postcolonial Nigeria and The Mimic Men in the Caribbean.

items.title: Q58 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Golding, R. M. Ballantyne
items.stem:
Which two names from R.M. Ballantyne's Coral Island are repeated in William Golding's reworking of the same text as Lord of the Flies?
(a) Ralph
(b) Roger
(c) Jack
(d) Simon
The correct option is :
items.explanation: R. M. Ballantyne's Victorian boys' adventure novel The Coral Island (1857) features three young castaways named Ralph Rover, Jack Martin, and Peterkin Gay. In his dark counter-narrative Lord of the Flies (1954), William Golding retains the names Ralph (a) and Jack (c) while replacing Peterkin with Piggy and Simon.

items.title: Q59 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Johnson, Joseph Addison, Robert Browning, John Keats
items.stem:
Which two of the following poems can be categorized as poems belonging to the neo-classical period of English literature.
(a) "The Ring and the Book"
(b) "The Vanity of Human Wishes"
(c) "Cato"
(d) "Lamia"
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Samuel Johnson's Juvenalian verse satire 'The Vanity of Human Wishes' (b, 1749) and Joseph Addison's verse tragedy Cato (c, 1713) belong to the eighteenth-century neoclassical period, whereas Keats's 'Lamia' (1820) is Romantic and Browning's The Ring and the Book (1868–69) is Victorian.

items.title: Q60 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem:
In Paradise Lost Milton invokes his 'Heavenly Muse', 'Urania', at the beginning of which two books?
(a) Book I
(b) Book IV
(c) Book IX
(d) Book VII
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: In Paradise Lost, John Milton invokes his 'Heavenly Muse' at the opening of Book I (a, 'Sing Heav'nly Muse') and explicitly addresses her by name as 'Urania' at the opening of Book VII (d, 'Descend from Heav'n Urania, by that name / If rightly thou art call'd').

items.title: Q61 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print · Unit II: Poetry · William Dunbar, Geoffrey Chaucer, John Gower, Robert Henryson
items.stem:
Which three of the following poets figure in William Dunbar's Lament for the Makers?
(a) Geoffrey Chaucer
(b) John Gower
(c) Robert Henryson
(d) William Langland
Choose the most appropriate option :
items.explanation: In his Middle Scots elegy 'Lament for the Makaris' (c. 1505) with its refrain Timor mortis conturbat me, William Dunbar mourns the deaths of Geoffrey Chaucer (a), John Gower (b), and fellow Scottish makar Robert Henryson (c), but does not mention William Langland.

items.title: Q62 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit II: Poetry · Gerard Manley Hopkins, James Joyce, Graham Greene, Stephen Spender
items.stem:
Examples of poetic compounding are found in the work of which two modernist writers?
(a) Graham Greene
(b) James Joyce
(c) Gerard Manley Hopkins
(d) Stephen Spender
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Bold lexical and poetic compounding is a hallmark of both Gerard Manley Hopkins (c, who coined compounds like 'dapple-dawn-drawn' and 'wanwood leafmeal') and James Joyce (b, whose modernist prose in Ulysses and Finnegans Wake abounds in compound neologisms).

items.title: Q63 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Arnold Wesker, Shelagh Delaney, John Osborne, John Arden
items.stem:
Which three of the following writers are associated with 'kitchen sink drama'?
(a) Arnold Wesker
(b) John Arden
(c) Shelagh Delaney
(d) John Osborne
Choose the most appropriate option:
items.explanation: Arnold Wesker (a, Roots), Shelagh Delaney (c, A Taste of Honey), and John Osborne (d, Look Back in Anger) are central playwrights of British 'kitchen sink drama' of the late 1950s, which depicted gritty working-class domestic life.

items.title: Q64 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit I: Drama · John Heywood, Thomas Heywood, Thomas Kyd
items.stem:
Which two of the following plays were written by Thomas Heywood?
(a) Gorboduc
(b) The Play Called the Four P.P.
(c) The Play of the Weather
(d) The Spanish Tragedy
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: The Tudor interludes The Play Called the Four PP (b) and The Play of the Weather (c) were written by sixteenth-century dramatist John Heywood (printed as Thomas Heywood in the question). Gorboduc was written by Norton and Sackville, and The Spanish Tragedy by Thomas Kyd.

items.title: Q65 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
In the following list, which two actors belong to the Elizabethan period?
(a) Richard Burbage
(b) Will Kempe
(c) David Garrick
(d) John Kemble
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Tragedian Richard Burbage (a) and comic actor Will Kempe (b) were both famous Elizabethan performers and key members of Shakespeare's acting company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men. David Garrick and John Philip Kemble were eighteenth-century actors.

items.title: Q66 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Judith Butler, Barbara Johnson, Elaine Showalter, Camille Paglia
items.stem:
Match the works with authors :
(a) Bodies that Matter — (i) Camille Paglia
(b) A World of Difference — (ii) Elaine Showalter
(c) A Literature of their Own — (iii) Barbara Johnson
(d) Vamps and Tramps — (iv) Judith Butler
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Bodies That Matter (1993) was written by Judith Butler (a-iv), A World of Difference (1987) by deconstructionist critic Barbara Johnson (b-iii), A Literature of Their Own (1977) by Elaine Showalter (c-ii), and Vamps & Tramps (1994) by Camille Paglia (d-i).

items.title: Q67 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Homi K. Bhabha, Geoffrey Hartman, Edward Said, Julia Kristeva
items.stem:
Match the works with authors :
(a) Homi Bhabha — (i) Saving the Text
(b) Geoffrey Hartman — (ii) The Location of Culture
(c) Edward Said — (iii) Desire in Language
(d) Julia Kristeva — (iv) Culture and Imperialism
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Homi K. Bhabha authored The Location of Culture (a-ii, 1994), Geoffrey Hartman authored Saving the Text (b-i, 1981), Edward Said authored Culture and Imperialism (c-iv, 1993), and Julia Kristeva authored Desire in Language (d-iii, 1980).

items.title: Q68 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Samuel Johnson, David Masson, Richard Steele, Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Match the periodicals with their writers / contributors :
(a) The Rambler — (i) Charles Dickens
(b) Macmillan's Magazine — (ii) Samuel Johnson
(c) The Guardian — (iii) David Masson
(d) Bentley's Miscellany — (iv) Richard Steele
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Samuel Johnson founded and wrote The Rambler (a-ii, 1750–1752); Scottish scholar David Masson was the first editor of Macmillan's Magazine (b-iii, founded 1859); Richard Steele founded The Guardian (c-iv, 1713); and Charles Dickens served as the first editor of Bentley's Miscellany (d-i, 1837–1839), where Oliver Twist was serialized.

items.title: Q69 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · John Fiske, Michel de Certeau, Pierre Bourdieu, Jean-François Lyotard
items.stem:
Match the theorist with the text :
(a) John Fiske — (i) Distinction
(b) Michel de Certeau — (ii) The Postmodern Condition
(c) Pierre Bourdieu — (iii) Reading the Popular
(d) Jean Francois Lyotard — (iv) The Practice of Everyday Life
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: John Fiske wrote Reading the Popular (a-iii, 1989), Michel de Certeau wrote The Practice of Everyday Life (b-iv, 1980), Pierre Bourdieu wrote Distinction (c-i, 1979), and Jean-Francois Lyotard wrote The Postmodern Condition (d-ii, 1979).

items.title: Q70 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Rita Kothari, Probal Dasgupta, Braj B. Kachru, Baljinder K. Mahal
items.stem:
Match the author with the text :
(a) Rita Kothari — (i) The Queen's Hinglish
(b) Probal Dasgupta — (ii) The Indianization of English
(c) Braj B. Kachru — (iii) Translating India
(d) Baljinder K. Mahal — (iv) The Otherness of English
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Rita Kothari wrote Translating India (a-iii, 2003), Probal Dasgupta wrote The Otherness of English (b-iv, 1993), Braj B. Kachru wrote The Indianization of English (c-ii, 1983), and Baljinder K. Mahal wrote The Queen's Hinglish (d-i, 2006).

items.title: Q71 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Match the following technological advancements impacting learning and teaching of language with their corresponding years:
(a) Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) — (i) 2004
(b) Streaming of Video on the Internet — (ii) 2003
(c) MySpace.com — (iii) 1991
(d) Facebook — (iv) 1997
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) was first publicly released by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 (a-iii), commercial video streaming on the internet emerged in 1997 (b-iv), MySpace.com was launched in 2003 (c-ii), and Facebook was founded in 2004 (d-i).

items.title: Q72 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Match the types of writing with their descriptions:
(a) exegesis — (i) writing about saints' lives
(b) invective — (ii) detailed explanation of a passage
(c) hagiography — (iii) a defence or justification of one's actions and beliefs
(d) apology — (iv) a bitterly critical attack of something
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Exegesis is a critical explanation or interpretation of a text (a-ii); invective is a fiercely abusive or critical attack (b-iv); hagiography is the biography of saints' lives (c-i); and an apology (apologia) is a formal defence of one's actions or beliefs (d-iii).

items.title: Q73 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Edgar Allan Poe, E. M. Forster, Katherine Mansfield, Salman Rushdie
items.stem:
Match the author with the story:
(a) Edgar Allan Poe — (i) "The Fall of the House of Usher"
(b) E.M. Forster — (ii) "The Prophet's Hair"
(c) Katherine Mansfield — (iii) "The Garden Party"
(d) Salman Rushdie — (iv) "The Celestial Omnibus"
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Edgar Allan Poe wrote the gothic tale 'The Fall of the House of Usher' (a-i, 1839), E. M. Forster wrote 'The Celestial Omnibus' (b-iv, 1911), Katherine Mansfield wrote 'The Garden Party' (c-iii, 1922), and Salman Rushdie wrote 'The Prophet's Hair' (d-ii, in East, West, 1994).

items.title: Q74 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Percy Bysshe Shelley, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, John Keats, William Wordsworth
items.stem:
Match the poet with the opening line of the poem.
(a) Shelley — (i) I cry your mercy — pity — love! — aye, love!
(b) Coleridge — (ii) The world is too much with us
(c) Keats — (iii) O world, O life, O time
(d) Wordsworth — (iv) When true love burns desire is Love's pure flame
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: P. B. Shelley's 'A Lament' opens with 'O world! O life! O time!' (a-iii); S. T. Coleridge's 'Desire' opens with 'Where true Love burns Desire is Love's pure flame' (b-iv); John Keats's sonnet to Fanny Brawne begins 'I cry your mercy—pity—love!—aye, love!' (c-i); and William Wordsworth's sonnet begins 'The world is too much with us' (d-ii).

items.title: Q75 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Match the characters with the play :
(a) Donalbain — (i) King Lear
(b) Claudio — (ii) Macbeth
(c) Nerissa — (iii) Merchant of Venice
(d) Goneril — (iv) Measure for Measure
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: In Shakespeare's plays, Donalbain is King Duncan's younger son in Macbeth (a-ii), Claudio is Isabella's brother in Measure for Measure (b-iv), Nerissa is Portia's waiting-gentlewoman in The Merchant of Venice (c-iii), and Goneril is King Lear's eldest daughter in King Lear (d-i).

items.title: Q76 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Sigmund Freud, Ferdinand de Saussure, Cleanth Brooks, Jacques Derrida
items.stem: The following is a list of key critical terms. Which is the right chronological order of their formulation?
options: Langue — the unconscious — differance — heresy of paraphrase
The unconscious — langue — heresy of paraphrase — differance
Differance — langue — heresy of paraphrase — the unconscious
Langue — differance — the unconscious — heresy of paraphrase
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence of formulation is: Sigmund Freud's 'the unconscious' (c. 1895–1900, The Interpretation of Dreams), Ferdinand de Saussure's 'langue' (1906–1911 lectures; Course in General Linguistics, 1916), Cleanth Brooks's 'heresy of paraphrase' (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947), and Jacques Derrida's 'différance' (1963/1968).

items.title: Q77 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Noam Chomsky
items.stem:
What is the order of publication of the following books of Noam Chomsky?
(a) Problems of Knowledge and Freedom
(b) Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
(c) Syntactic Structures
(d) Knowledge of Language
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication of Noam Chomsky's books is: Syntactic Structures (c, 1957), Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (b, 1965), Problems of Knowledge and Freedom (a, 1971), and Knowledge of Language (d, 1986).

items.title: Q78 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Rasmus Rask, Franz Bopp, Jacob Grimm
items.stem:
What is the correct chronological order of the publication of the following?
(a) German Grammar (Jacob Grimm)
(b) Comparative Grammar of Sanskrit, Zend, Greek, Latin, Lithuanian, Gothic and German (Franz Bopp)
(c) An Investigation into the Origin of Old Norse or Icelandic Language (Rasmus Rask)
(d) Concerning the Conjugation System of the Sanskrit Language in Comparison with those of the Greek, Latin, Persian and German Languages (Franz Bopp)
items.explanation: Rasmus Rask completed his prize essay An Investigation into the Origin of the Old Norse or Icelandic Language in 1814 (published 1818) (c), followed by Franz Bopp's On the Conjugation System of the Sanskrit Language (1816) (d), Jacob Grimm's Deutsche Grammatik (German Grammar, 1819) (a), and Franz Bopp's Comparative Grammar (1833) (b).

items.title: Q79 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Richard Steele, Joseph Addison, Jonathan Swift, Leigh Hunt
items.stem:
What is the Chronological order of the appearance of the following periodicals?
(a) The Tatler
(b) The Spectator
(c) The Examiner
(d) The Reflector
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: The chronological order of appearance is: Richard Steele's The Tatler (a, April 1709), Addison and Steele's The Spectator (b, March 1711), Jonathan Swift's Tory periodical The Examiner (c, August 1710 / or Leigh Hunt's The Examiner, 1808), and Leigh Hunt's quarterly magazine The Reflector (d, 1810–1811).

items.title: Q80 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · John Milton, Daniel Defoe, Jonathan Swift, Edmund Burke
items.stem: Which of the following arrangements of prose-pamphlets is in the right chronological order?
options: The Shortest Way with Dissenters — A Modest Proposal — Areopagitica — Reflections on the Revolution in France
A Modest Proposal — The Shortest Way with Dissenters — Areopagitica — Reflections on the Revolution in France
Areopagitica — The Shortest Way with Dissenters — A Modest Proposal — Reflections on the Revolution in France
Areopagitica — Reflections on the Revolution in France — The Shortest Way with Dissenters — A Modest Proposal
items.explanation: The correct chronological order of these prose pamphlets is: John Milton's Areopagitica (1644), Daniel Defoe's The Shortest Way with the Dissenters (1702), Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal (1729), and Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790).

items.title: Q81 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Daniel Defoe, Laurence Sterne, Charles Dickens, James Joyce
items.stem: Which of the following fictional characters is in the right Chronological order?
options: Uncle Toby — Man Friday — Stephen Dedalus — Miss Havisham
Stephen Dedalus — Man Friday — Uncle Toby — Miss Havisham
Man Friday — Uncle Toby — Miss Havisham — Stephen Dedalus
Miss Havisham — Uncle Toby — Stephen Dedalus — Man Friday
items.explanation: The correct chronological order by novel publication is: Man Friday in Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719), Uncle Toby in Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy (1759–1767), Miss Havisham in Charles Dickens's Great Expectations (1860–1861), and Stephen Dedalus in James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916).

items.title: Q82 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Which of the following set of characters in Charles Dickens' novels is in the right chronological order?
options: Mr. Bounderby — David Copperfield — Mrs. Mann — Nathaniel Winkle
David Copperfield — Mr. Bounderby — Nathaniel Winkle — Mrs. Mann
Nathaniel Winkle — Mrs. Mann — David Copperfield — Mr. Bounderby
Mrs. Mann — David Copperfield — Nathaniel Winkle — Mr. Bounderby
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence across Charles Dickens's novels is: Nathaniel Winkle in The Pickwick Papers (1836–1837), Mrs. Mann in Oliver Twist (1837–1839), David Copperfield in David Copperfield (1849–1850), and Josiah Bounderby in Hard Times (1854).

items.title: Q83 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · D. H. Lawrence
items.stem: Which arrangement of D.H. Lawrence's novels is in the correct chronological sequence?
options: Kangaroo — The Plumed Serpent — Sons and Lovers — The Rainbow
Sons and Lovers — The Rainbow — Kangaroo — The Plumed Serpent
The Rainbow — The Plumed Serpent — Kangaroo — Sons and Lovers
The Rainbow — Kangaroo — The Plumed Serpent — Sons and Lovers
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence of D. H. Lawrence's novels by publication year is: Sons and Lovers (1913), The Rainbow (1915), Kangaroo (1923), and The Plumed Serpent (1926).

items.title: Q84 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton, Alexander Pope, Percy Bysshe Shelley, John Keats
items.stem: Which of the following is the correct chronological order of publication of the following poems?
options: Lamia — Paradise Lost — Alastor — The Dunciad
The Dunciad — Alastor — Lamia — Paradise Lost
Alastor — The Dunciad — Paradise Lost — Lamia
Paradise Lost — The Dunciad — Alastor — Lamia
items.explanation: The correct chronological order of publication is: John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667), Alexander Pope's The Dunciad (1728), Percy Bysshe Shelley's Alastor, or The Spirit of Solitude (1816), and John Keats's Lamia (1820).

items.title: Q85 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit I: Drama · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Which of the following plays by T.S. Eliot is in the correct chronological order of publication?
options: Murder in the Cathedral — The Family Reunion — The Cocktail Party — The Confidential Clerk
The Cocktail Party — The Confidential Clerk — The Family Reunion — Murder in the Cathedral
The Family Reunion — The Cocktail Party — Murder in the Cathedral — The Confidential Clerk
The Confidential Clerk — Murder in the Cathedral — The Cocktail Party — The Family Reunion
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence of T. S. Eliot's verse plays is: Murder in the Cathedral (1935), The Family Reunion (1939), The Cocktail Party (1949), and The Confidential Clerk (1953).

items.title: Q86 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Given below are two statements :— Assertion (A) and Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : Only actual research develops research skills.
Reason (R) : Information is discrete, whereas knowledge consists of a network of connections.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are independently true: hands-on practice is essential to develop research skills, and knowledge is an interconnected network rather than isolated facts. However, the distinction between information and knowledge does not directly explain why only practical research builds research skills.

items.title: Q87 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Mikhail Bakhtin
items.stem:
Given below are two statements :— Assertion (A) and Reason (R):
Assertion (A) : The Primary component in novelistic forms is a plot that evolves coherently from its beginning to an end in which all complications are resolved.
Reason (R) : The novel is constituted by a multiplicity of divergent and contending social voices that achieve their full significance only in the process of their dialogic interaction both with each other and with the voice of the narrator.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Assertion (A) is false because novelistic forms are not defined simply by a closed, fully resolved plot. Reason (R) is true and states Mikhail Bakhtin's concept of 'heteroglossia' and dialogism, whereby the novel is shaped by competing social voices interacting with the narrator.

items.title: Q88 · Dec 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies

Given below are two statements :— Assertion (A) and Reason (R):

Reason (R) : A dialect describes variations not only at the phonological level, but also at the levels of lexis and syntax.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Both statements are true in sociolinguistics: dialects encompass both regional and social varieties (sociolects), and unlike an accent (which is purely phonological), a dialect involves lexical, morphological, and syntactic variations. However, (R) defines the linguistic levels of a dialect rather than explaining why dialects span social and regional groups.

Read the following poem and answer the questions :

HOME IS SO SAD
Home is so sad. It stays as it was left,
Shaped to the comfort of the last to go
As if to win them back. Instead, bereft
Of anyone to please, it withers so,
Having no heart to put aside the theft

And turn again to what it started as,
A joyous shot at how things ought to be,
Long fallen wide. You can see how it was :
Look at the pictures and the cutlery.
The music in the piano stool. That Vase.

Why is the 'home' 'Sad'?
options: Because it has waited in vain
Because it is devoid of residents
items.explanation: In Philip Larkin's poem 'Home is so Sad' (from The Whitsun Weddings, 1964), the home is sad because its former inhabitants have departed and left it empty ('bereft / Of anyone to please'), devoid of residents.

items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions :

Lying is an accursed vice. It is only our words which bind us together and make us human. If we realized the horror and weight of lying, we would see that it is more worthy of the stake than other crimes. I find that people normally waste time quite inappropriately punishing children for innocent misdemeanours, tormenting them for thoughtless actions which lead nowhere and leave no trace. It seems to me that the only faults which we should vigorously attack as soon as they arise and start to develop are lying and, a little below that, stubbornness. Those faults grow up with the children. Once let the tongue acquire the habit of lying and it is astonishing how impossible it is to make it give it up. That is why some otherwise decent men are abject slaves to it. One of my tailors is a good enough fellow, but I have never heard him once speak the truth, not even when it would help him, if he did so.

How does 'lying' affect human relationships?
options: It reduces the affinity among people
It promotes togetherness among diverse people
It does not affect at all as it is merely words.
items.explanation: In this passage from Michel de Montaigne's essay 'Of Liars', the author states that 'It is only our words which bind us together and make us human.' Consequently, lying corrupts the bond of mutual trust and reduces the affinity among people.

Read the following passage from Antigone and answer the question :

Creon : And yet wert bold enough to break the law.
Antigone : Yea, for these laws were not ordained by Zeus,
And she who sits enthroned with gods below,
Justice, enacted not these human laws.
Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man,
Could'st by a breath annul and override
The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.

The three kinds of laws implicit in Antigone's response are :
options: Of Gods, of Zeus, of Justice
Of Gods, of Justice, of Man
Of Man, of Heaven, of Zeus
items.explanation: In this speech from Sophocles' Antigone, Antigone contrasts three domains of law: the divine laws of the Gods (Zeus and the immutable unwritten laws of Heaven), the chthonic law of Justice ('she who sits enthroned with gods below'), and the mortal decrees of Man (Creon's 'human laws').
